## Slide 5 — Course overview

**On slide**

Course overview

- Formulating sequential decisions and understanding returns and values

- Learning with tabular methods and function approximation

- Deep value learning and policy optimization

- Exploration, planning and learned models

- Offline RL and RL for LLM post-training

![Picture 4](<nuts_and_bolts_chatgpt_assets/8e89392bc87b9d166983c228dbd03871f0d4fc4511df92a3387341fca9224d6d.jpeg>)

**Speaker notes**

Suggested delivery: 1:00

The goal is to understand the ideas shared by RL methods and to design and evaluate learning agents. The course moves from foundations toward modern methods. Use the map for orientation without explaining the algorithms yet.

Source: course/syllabus/syllabusFall26.docx (instructor-frozen September 29, 2026). Course policies remain governed by that syllabus.

## Slide 6 — Preparation

**On slide**

Preparation

- AI background: agents, decisions, utility, states, actions and rewards

- ML background: regression, stochastic gradient descent and neural networks

- Working knowledge of probability, statistics and linear algebra

- Python programming, including translating equations into code

- Prior deep learning coursework is helpful but not required

**Speaker notes**

Suggested delivery: 1:15

Refer to the syllabus for the COMP341 and COMP421/521 prerequisites and the distinctions between formal prerequisites and expected background. Encourage students to assess gaps early and discuss concerns before add/drop. Assignments involve substantial programming and mathematical reasoning.

## Slide 10 — Assessment

**On slide**

Assessment

- Four assignments planned, with the lowest dropped. The count may change. If more than three are offered, the lowest is dropped

- Each midterm covers a different set of topics

- No final exam

| Component | Course grade |
| --- | --- |
| Individual programming assignments | 20% |
| Three midterms, 15% each | 45% |
| Semester project | 35% |

**Speaker notes**

Suggested delivery: 1:45

Assignments provide practice in implementation and experimental reasoning. Exams assess understanding of the taught material. Exact dates and instructions will follow through course communication. Do not turn internal week targets into announced dates.

Source: course/syllabus/syllabusFall26.docx (instructor-frozen September 29, 2026). Course policies remain governed by that syllabus.

## Slide 11 — Semester project

**On slide**

Semester project

Formulate an RL problem, build a solution, compare with a meaningful baseline and evaluate the results.

| Milestone | Course grade |
| --- | --- |
| Proposal | 5% |
| Formulation and design | 5% |
| Progress and evaluation | 7.5% |
| Presentation | 7.5% |
| Final report | 10% |

Teams of 2–3 encouraged. Individual and four-person teams considered case by case.

**Speaker notes**

Suggested delivery: 2:00

Project expectations scale with team size. A well-supported negative result can succeed. Novelty and benchmark superiority are not required. Communicate limitations as well as results. Further project details will follow during the semester.

Source: course/syllabus/syllabusFall26.docx (instructor-frozen September 29, 2026). Course policies remain governed by that syllabus.

## Slide 12 — LLM use in coursework

**On slide**

LLM use in coursework

- LLMs may help with coding and reports, with disclosure

- Failure to disclose use is treated as plagiarism

- You must understand, check and explain submitted work

- You remain responsible for errors

- An LLM-use report is required for every assignment and report

- One-shot or few-shot delegation of an assignment solution receives no credit

**Speaker notes**

Suggested delivery: 2:00

The report requirements will be provided before the first assignment/report. The assignment no-credit rule applies specifically to assignment solutions. Do not extend it to project coding or introduce a prompt-count threshold as a grading rubric. Understanding and verification remain the student's responsibility.

Source: course/syllabus/syllabusFall26.docx (instructor-frozen September 29, 2026). Course policies remain governed by that syllabus.

## Slide 13 — Writing and exams

**On slide**

Writing and exams

- Project reports should be clear, focused and concise

- Verbose, repetitive, unnecessarily detailed, unfocused, vague or obvious AI writing loses marks

- LLMs are not permitted in online or take-home midterms

- University rules on plagiarism and academic conduct apply

## Slide 14 — Submissions and late policy

**On slide**

Submissions and late policy

- Submit through KU Hub. Email submissions are not accepted

- Download and check your uploaded files. Only the latest submission is graded

- Ten late days in total, at most three per submission except the final report

- Remaining late days may be used for the final report, with a possible Incomplete grade

- Exceeding the late-day limits incurs grade penalties

Full make-up and early-exam policies appear in the syllabus.

**Speaker notes**

Suggested delivery: 2:00

The server timestamp determines submission time. An appropriate extension will be granted if the system is down. Do not invent a numerical late penalty.
